short_description: Italian dual-use (civil/defense) X-band SAR constellation, 1st generation (4 satellites, 2007-2010) plus 2nd generation satellites, up to ~1 m resolution in Spotlight mode.
long_description: COSMO-SkyMed (COnstellation of small Satellites for the Mediterranean basin Observation) is ASI's X-band SAR constellation, operated for both civil and defense applications. The first generation (4 identical satellites launched 2007-2010) provides resolutions from ~1 m (Spotlight) to ~100 m (ScanSAR/Huge Region), with very short revisit thanks to the 4-satellite constellation. A second generation (CSG) began launching in 2019 with improved SAR performance and additional polarimetric/interferometric capabilities. Commercial/institutional access is more restricted than Sentinel-1 — typically via ASI/e-GEOS for tasked, high-resolution acquisitions.

known_limitations: Access/licensing is more restrictive than Sentinel-1; very high resolution modes have narrow swath, trading area coverage for detail.
example_use_cases: High-resolution InSAR for infrastructure monitoring (bridges, dams); emergency response tasking (floods, earthquakes) at fine detail.

short_description: Added a 15 m panchromatic band and onboard calibration to the TM design; still operating today but affected by a scan line corrector failure since 2003 that leaves data gaps in each scene.
long_description: Landsat 7's ETM+ improved on Landsat 4/5's TM with a 15 m panchromatic band, better radiometric calibration, and a higher-resolution thermal band (60 m vs 120 m). In May 2003 its Scan Line Corrector (SLC) failed, causing a "zig-zag" wedge pattern of missing data (~22% of each scene) that remains present in every acquisition since — data is still useful, especially with gap-filling algorithms, but must be handled explicitly unlike gap-free sensors. Landsat 7 has been in a lowered/drifting orbit since 2022 to preserve fuel, coordinated with Landsat 9's orbit.
spatial_resolution_summary: 30 m (VIS/NIR/SWIR), 15 m (pan), 60 m (thermal)
notes: Always check for the SLC-off gap pattern before using a scene for precise area calculations; gap-filled composites exist but introduce interpolation artifacts.
known_limitations: SLC-off gaps (~22% missing data per scene) since 2003; orbit has been drifting since 2022.
example_use_cases: Continuity dataset alongside Landsat 8/9 for 16-day combined revisit.

sensor_name: OLI/TIRS (Operational Land Imager / Thermal Infrared Sensor)
short_description: Two-instrument push-broom sensor (OLI for reflective bands, TIRS for thermal) with improved SNR and 12-bit radiometry over earlier Landsats.
long_description: Landsat 8 introduced a push-broom design (vs the whisk-broom scanning of earlier Landsats), split across two instruments: OLI (Operational Land Imager) for the visible/NIR/SWIR/panchromatic bands, and TIRS (Thermal Infrared Sensor) for two thermal bands. It added a coastal/aerosol band and a cirrus-detection band not present on Landsat 7, and improved radiometric resolution to 12 bit, giving much better sensitivity in dark targets (water, shadow) than the 8-bit TM/ETM+ series.
spatial_resolution_summary: 30 m (VIS/NIR/SWIR), 15 m (pan), 100 m (thermal, resampled to 30 m in products)
download_snippet:
# Using the USGS M2M API or, more commonly, via pystac-client against
# the USGS Landsat STAC endpoint / AWS Landsat public bucket.
import pystac_client
catalog = pystac_client.Client.open("https://landsatlook.usgs.gov/stac-server")
search = catalog.search(
    collections=["landsat-c2l2-sr"],
    bbox=[12.4, 41.8, 12.6, 42.0],
    datetime="2024-06-01/2024-08-31",
)
items = list(search.items())
print(len(items))
notes: Collection 2 Level-2 products come with QA_PIXEL cloud/shadow masks — always apply them before compositing. Coverage stops around ±81° latitude — a real orbital/tiling-grid limit (not a metadata gap), so true polar ice sheets fall outside the systematic acquisition mask.
known_limitations: TIRS has a known stray-light issue affecting some thermal band calibration; USGS provides correction guidance.
example_use_cases: General-purpose 30m land monitoring, NDVI time series, LST retrieval.

short_description: Near-identical successor to Landsat 8 with improved radiometric resolution (14 bit) and a better-calibrated thermal sensor; flies 8 days out of phase with Landsat 8 for combined 8-day revisit.

import pystac_client
catalog = pystac_client.Client.open("https://landsatlook.usgs.gov/stac-server")
search = catalog.search(
    collections=["landsat-c2l2-sr"],
    bbox=[12.4, 41.8, 12.6, 42.0],
    datetime="2024-06-01/2024-08-31",
    query={"platform": {"eq": "LANDSAT_9"}},
)
items = list(search.items())
print(len(items))

example_use_cases: High-frequency 30m land monitoring when combined with Landsat 8.

sensor_name: SEVIRI (Spinning Enhanced Visible and InfraRed Imager)
short_description: Meteosat Second Generation geostationary satellite carrying SEVIRI, imaging Europe/Africa/Atlantic every 15 minutes across 12 channels.
long_description: Meteosat-10 is part of the Meteosat Second Generation (MSG) series operated by EUMETSAT from geostationary orbit (0° or shifted longitude depending on operational role: prime, rapid-scan, or in-orbit backup). Its SEVIRI instrument images the full Earth disc (Europe, Africa, Atlantic, Indian Ocean) every 15 minutes across 12 spectral channels (11 narrow-band + 1 high-resolution visible), the backbone dataset for short-term weather forecasting (nowcasting), severe storm tracking, and fire/dust detection over the EUMETSAT coverage area.
spatial_resolution_summary: 3 km at nadir (1 km for the HRV broadband channel)
geographic_coverage: Europe, Africa, Atlantic, Indian Ocean (full disc)
notes: Operational role (prime imaging, rapid scan, or backup) rotates between MSG satellites over time — check EUMETSAT's current operational status page for which Meteosat-10 role is active before assuming continuous archive availability under this exact satellite.
known_limitations: 3 km resolution at nadir degrades toward the edge of the disc (geostationary viewing geometry).
example_use_cases: Short-term nowcasting; severe convective storm tracking; Saharan dust/volcanic ash detection.

short_description: Italian hyperspectral mission with ~239 contiguous VNIR/SWIR bands at 30 m, plus a 5 m panchromatic band, aimed at detailed material/vegetation spectral characterization.
long_description: PRISMA (PRecursore IperSpettrale della Missione Applicativa) is ASI's hyperspectral Earth observation satellite, acquiring ~239 narrow, contiguous spectral bands across VNIR (400-1010 nm) and SWIR (920-2505 nm) at 30 m resolution, alongside a 5 m panchromatic band for sharpening. Unlike multispectral sensors (Sentinel-2, Landsat) with a handful of broad bands, PRISMA's dense spectral sampling supports detailed material identification — mineral mapping, precision agriculture (crop stress/nutrient status), water quality, and soil properties — at the cost of a narrow ~30 km swath and tasked (not continuous global) acquisition.
spatial_resolution_summary: 30 m (hyperspectral, ~239 bands), 5 m (panchromatic)
temporal_resolution: ~7 days revisit at target (tasked acquisition, not continuous)
notes: This record lists a representative subset (44 of ~239 total bands, evenly sampled) so the spectral chart is readable — real PRISMA products have contiguous ~9-12 nm-spaced bands across the full VNIR (400-1010 nm) and SWIR (920-2505 nm) ranges, not just these samples. Acquisitions must be tasked/ordered ahead of time for a specific area — it's not a wall-to-wall continuous archive like Sentinel-2. Plan requests with lead time.
known_limitations: Narrow 30km swath; tasked (not systematic) acquisition means gaps in temporal coverage for a given area.
example_use_cases: Precision agriculture crop stress mapping; mineral/geological mapping; detailed water quality analysis.

short_description: C-band synthetic aperture radar constellation, the main operational source for interferometry (ground deformation) and all-weather day/night monitoring.
long_description: Sentinel-1 is a constellation of C-band SAR satellites operated by ESA under the Copernicus programme. Because SAR is independent of cloud cover and solar illumination, it is the reference source for ground deformation monitoring (landslides, subsidence, earthquakes), flood mapping, and maritime surveillance. Sentinel-1A has been operational since 2014; Sentinel-1B stopped transmitting in December 2021 due to a failure, temporarily reducing revisit frequency until Sentinel-1C launched in December 2024 and restored the two-satellite constellation.
spatial_resolution_summary: 5x20 m in Interferometric Wide (IW) mode, the most commonly used
geographic_coverage: Global, ~81°S to ~81°N (priority to Europe and coastal areas)
download_snippet:
from sentinelhub import SHConfig, SentinelHubCatalog

config = SHConfig()
catalog = SentinelHubCatalog(config=config)
search_iterator = catalog.search(
    collection="sentinel-1-grd",
    bbox=[12.4, 41.8, 12.6, 42.0],
    time=("2024-01-01", "2024-02-01"),
)
for item in search_iterator:
    print(item["id"])
notes: Note: since 2023 data access has migrated from the old Copernicus Open Access Hub to the new Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem — old links/REST endpoints no longer work. For interferometry, start from SLC data (not GRD).
known_limitations: Speckle noise requires filtering before most analyses. Radiometric terrain correction (RTC) is not applied by default on GRD products — apply it yourself for quantitative backscatter comparisons across different terrain.
example_use_cases: Landslide and subsidence monitoring via InSAR time series; flood extent mapping during/after heavy rain events; ship detection in coastal waters.

qa.question: Can I use GRD products directly for interferometry, or do I need SLC?

replies.text: You need SLC (Single Look Complex) for InSAR — GRD has already lost the phase information during ground-range detection. Use GRD only for amplitude-based analyses (flood mapping, ship detection).

To add — SNAP's InSAR tutorials all start from SLC for exactly this reason. If you're looking for a quick coherence check without full InSAR processing, the pre-computed Coherence Map product also works and saves time.

short_description: 13-band multispectral optical constellation, the reference for NDVI and vegetation/land cover monitoring at 10-60 m resolution.
long_description: Sentinel-2 is a constellation of two optical satellites (2A since 2015, 2B since 2017) designed primarily for observing vegetation, soil, and inland/ coastal waters. The MSI sensor acquires 13 spectral bands from visible to short-wave infrared, at spatial resolutions of 10, 20, or 60 m depending on the band. It is the most widely used source for vegetation indices such as NDVI/EVI and for medium-to-high resolution land cover classification with frequent revisit.
spatial_resolution_summary: 10 m (VIS/NIR), 20 m (red edge/SWIR), 60 m (atmospheric bands)
temporal_resolution: 5 days (with the two-satellite constellation, at equator)
geographic_coverage: Global, ~81°S to ~81°N (land areas and coastal zones)
notes: Use the "Harmonized" collection on Google Earth Engine to avoid the radiometric offset introduced by processing baseline 04.00 (from late 2021 onward, raw non-harmonized values have a +1000 shift). Coverage stops around ±81° latitude — a real orbital/tiling-grid limit (not a metadata gap), so true polar ice sheets fall outside the systematic acquisition mask.
known_limitations: Optical sensor: no valid data under cloud cover, so revisit for a clear observation can be much longer than the nominal 5 days depending on season and location. Always apply a cloud mask (e.g. using the SCL band or s2cloudless).
example_use_cases: Crop monitoring and vegetation health via NDVI time series; burned area mapping after wildfires; land cover change detection over multi-year periods.

short_description: Ocean/land color (OLCI) and dual-view thermal (SLSTR) constellation, built primarily for ocean and large-scale land/vegetation monitoring.
long_description: Sentinel-3 combines two main instruments: OLCI (Ocean and Land Colour Instrument), a 21-band medium-resolution optical imager descended from ENVISAT's MERIS, and SLSTR (Sea and Land Surface Temperature Radiometer), a dual-view thermal instrument for accurate sea/land surface temperature. It also carries a radar altimeter for sea surface height. Coarser resolution than Sentinel-2 (300 m OLCI, 500m-1km SLSTR) but with daily-to-sub-daily global revisit, making it complementary rather than a substitute for Sentinel-2 in land applications.
spatial_resolution_summary: 300 m (OLCI), 500 m-1 km (SLSTR)
notes: Good complement to Sentinel-2 for daily large-area monitoring where 300m resolution is acceptable (e.g. regional vegetation trends, SST anomalies).
known_limitations: Coarse resolution vs Sentinel-2 — not suitable for field-scale analysis.
example_use_cases: Ocean color/chlorophyll monitoring; large-area LST anomaly detection.
